hook.text: In the Fertile Crescent, wild wheat grew thick. Someone decided to plant it near home. Everything changed.

buildup.text: The Neolithic revolution was the shift from foraging to farming, beginning around 12,000 years ago in multiple regions.

discovery.text: Domesticating plants and animals allowed food surplus, permanent villages, and rapid population growth.

twist.text: The shift wasn't a choice for progress. Climate change, population pressure, or depleted game may have forced it.

climax.text: The Neolithic revolution created the conditions for cities, states, writing, and inequality. It remade the world.

punchline.text: Farming didn't free us — it chained us to the land.

quiz.question: What did the Neolithic revolution involve?
options: The shift from foraging to farming

details.summary: The Neolithic Revolution was the transition from foraging to farming beginning around 12,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent. Domesticating plants and animals transformed human societies fundamentally, enabling permanent settlements, population growth, and social complexity.
details.whyItMatters: The shift to agriculture is arguably the most consequential event in human history. It made civilization possible but also introduced inequality, disease, environmental degradation, and labor burdens that foragers never experienced.
takeaways: The Neolithic Revolution began around 12,000 years ago
Farming enabled settlements, population growth, and social complexity
It also introduced inequality, disease, and environmental degradation

faq.question: Why did humans adopt agriculture if foraging was easier?
faq.answer: This remains debated. Climate change, population pressure, and social competition are leading theories. Foragers actually worked fewer hours with more varied diets. Agriculture may not have been a conscious choice but a gradual process that became irreversible as populations grew.

faq.question: Did agriculture develop independently in multiple places?
faq.answer: Yes. At least seven independent centers of domestication have been identified — the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, eastern North America, sub-Saharan Africa, and New Guinea. Each developed different crops suited to local environments.
